name: Ethiopian Empire
capital: Mobile royal camps; Gondar (from 1636); Addis Ababa (from 1886)

location.value: The Ethiopian highlands and, at times, Eritrea and surrounding lowlands. Capitals included Gondar (1635–1855) and Addis Ababa (from 1889).

terrain.value: High mountains and plateaus that made the country hard to conquer, cut by deep gorges (the Blue Nile).

climate.value: Highland climate with seasonal rains. The 1973 Wollo famine helped trigger the 1974 revolution.

resources.value: Highland farming (teff, coffee), cattle, gold and salt (amole blocks used as money).

disasters.value: Famines, including the Great Famine of 1888–92 and the Wollo famine of 1973.

urbanisation.value: Mostly rural. Mobile royal camps until Gondar (1635). Addis Ababa was founded in 1886 and became the capital in 1889.

disease.value: Not documented in the sources checked.

migration.value: The Oromo migrations (16th century) reshaped the population.

economicBase.value: Highland agriculture worked by peasants owing tribute to nobles and the church.

tradeRoutes.value: Trade via the Red Sea, coffee exports, and the Addis Ababa–Djibouti railway (1917).

wealth.value: No GDP figure is given in the sources checked.

moneyAndTax.value: Salt blocks, the Maria Theresa thaler, and from 1894 the Ethiopian birr. The Bank of Abyssinia was founded in 1905.

inequality.value: Emperor, nobility and church held land, over tribute-paying peasants. Slavery existed until it was abolished (1942).

governmentType.value: An absolute monarchy (to 1931), then a constitutional monarchy under the 1931 constitution, though power stayed with the emperor.

keyRulers.value: Yekuno Amlak (1270, founder of the Solomonic dynasty). Amda Seyon I. Zara Yaqob (1434–1468, peak). Tewodros II. Menelik II (1889–1913). Haile Selassie (1930–1974, last).

succession.value: Hereditary in the Solomonic dynasty (which claimed descent from Solomon and the Queen of Sheba), often contested.

institutions.value: The Ethiopian Orthodox Church, the 1931 constitution, and a parliament (1931–1974).

stability.value: The “Zemene Mesafint” (Era of the Princes, 1769–1855), when the emperor was a figurehead. The 1974 revolution.

eliteConflict.value: Regional lords competed with the emperor, especially during the Zemene Mesafint.

armyAndTech.value: Large feudal armies. Menelik II bought modern rifles and artillery, which made the victory at Adwa possible.

majorWars.value: The Ethiopian–Adal War (1529–1543). Ottoman–Ethiopian wars. Menelik II’s expansion. Victory over Italy at Adwa (1896). Italian invasion and occupation (1935–1941).

territoryChange.value: Expanded to roughly modern borders under Menelik II (1878–1904). Federated with Eritrea (1952). About 1.22 million km² (1954).

alliancesRivals.value: Rivals: the Adal Sultanate, the Ottomans, Egypt, the Mahdists and Italy. Portuguese help in the 1540s. British help to expel Italy (1941).

inventions.value: Rock-hewn churches (Lalibela, from the earlier Zagwe era) and the Gondar castles (Fasil Ghebbi). Modernisation under Menelik II and Haile Selassie (telephone, railway).

scienceEducation.value: Church schools and Geʿez learning, then modern schools from the early 20th century.

openness.value: Diplomatic ties with Portugal and Europe. Briefly Catholic (1622–1632) before expelling the Jesuits.

religion.value: Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Christianity (Catholic 1622–1632), plus Muslim, Jewish (Beta Israel) and traditional religion minorities.

languageWriting.value: Amharic (court and official), and Geʿez (liturgy and literature), in the Geʿez script.

artsArchitecture.value: The Kebra Nagast (14th-century epic), church paintings and manuscripts, and the castles of Gondar.

socialStructure.value: Emperor, nobility, clergy, peasants and slaves.

sharedIdentity.value: Christian Solomonic kingship. The Adwa victory made Ethiopia a symbol of African independence.

neighbours.value: The Adal Sultanate, the Ottomans, Egypt, Sudan, Somali states, and Italian, British and French colonies.

ideasReligions.value: A symbol of African independence and Pan-Africanism, and a founding member of the Organisation of African Unity (Addis Ababa, 1963).

colonisation.value: Never fully colonised. It defeated Italy at Adwa (1896), but was occupied by Italy (1936–1941). It expanded by conquest under Menelik II.

riseSignals.value: The Solomonic restoration (1270), and expansion under Amda Seyon I and Dawit I.

peakPeriod.value: The reign of Zara Yaqob (1434–1468). A modern revival under Menelik II (Adwa, 1896).

declineSignals.value: The Adal war, the Era of the Princes, the Italian occupation, and later famine, slow reform and unrest.

outcome.value: Revolution. The military Derg deposed Haile Selassie on 12 September 1974 and abolished the monarchy in March 1975.

sources.value: Royal chronicles in Geʿez, church records, and European and Arabic accounts. Checked against Wikipedia on 6 Nov 2026 (the infobox was read word for word; the body was summarised). See also Marcus (2002).

overallCertainty.value: Moderate to good. Some dates differ (e.g. Gondar 1635/1636, federation with Eritrea 1950/1952). The cause of Haile Selassie’s death (1975) is disputed.
